content:
You are planning a home addition, and somewhere in the back of your mind sits a question nobody asked out loud yet. Can your electrical panel actually handle it.

We have run this assessment on enough homes to know exactly which signs point to a panel that needs upgrading before construction begins. Here is what to look for before you break ground.

Why Panel Capacity Matters for a Home Addition

Every addition adds new demand to your home's electrical system, whether that means new outlets, lighting, or a full kitchen and bathroom. An older panel built for a smaller home often cannot support this added load safely.

Ignoring this step does not make the problem disappear. It means the issue surfaces mid construction instead, when it is far more expensive and disruptive to correct.

Warning Signs Your Panel Needs an Upgrade

Some signs show up well before construction begins, if you know where to look.

Frequent Breaker Trips

If breakers trip regularly under normal household use, your panel is likely already near capacity before any addition adds new demand to the system.

An Outdated Panel Rating

Panels rated below one hundred amps were common in older homes but rarely support the demands of a modern addition, especially one involving a kitchen, bathroom, or major appliances.

Flickering Lights During Appliance Use

Lights that dim or flicker when a major appliance runs are a sign the panel is struggling to distribute power evenly across your home's existing demand.

Warm Panel Covers or Discoloration

A panel cover that feels warm to the touch or shows discoloration around breakers can indicate overloading, which is a safety concern that should never wait for a convenient time to address.

What Happens If You Skip the Assessment

This is the scenario we see most often. A homeowner starts an addition without checking panel capacity, and an electrical inspector flags the issue mid construction, once new circuits are already planned into the build.

At that point, the panel upgrade becomes an urgent, unplanned expense layered on top of a project already underway, rather than a line item budgeted from the start. Materials already ordered for the original electrical plan sometimes need to be reconfigured entirely.

A Real Assessment, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa planned a primary suite addition without checking their existing panel capacity first. During the design phase, our electrical team identified an outdated panel rated well below what the new addition's kitchenette and bathroom would require.

Because the upgrade was identified before construction began, we built the panel replacement into the original project timeline and budget. The addition proceeded without a single mid construction surprise, and the inspection passed on the first review.

How to Get an Accurate Assessment Before You Build

I always advise clients to schedule an electrical assessment during the design phase of any addition, not after construction has already started. This single step prevents nearly every panel related surprise we encounter on active job sites.

A licensed electrician calculates your home's total projected load, including the new addition, and compares that number against your current panel's rated capacity. If the numbers do not align, the upgrade gets planned and priced before a single wall goes up.

Why We Handle Electrical and Construction Together

I prioritize a strategy where our electrical services team and our build services team assess every addition together from the very first site visit. This means panel capacity gets calculated alongside the addition's design, not discovered as a separate problem partway through construction.

If you are still working through what your addition will actually cost once every factor is accounted for, our earlier guide on room addition cost breaks down the full range of expenses homeowners should expect.

Final Thoughts

A home addition places new demand on a system that may already be near its limit. Watch for frequent breaker trips, an outdated panel rating, flickering lights, or a warm panel cover, and get an electrical assessment during the design phase, not after construction has already begun.

faqs.q: How do I know if my electrical panel needs an upgrade before an addition?
faqs.a: Frequent breaker trips, an outdated amperage rating, flickering lights, or a warm panel cover are all signs worth having assessed before construction begins.

faqs.q: What amperage panel do most modern additions require?
faqs.a: Most additions involving major appliances or a kitchen and bathroom require at least two hundred amps, though this depends on your home's total electrical demand.

faqs.q: How long does an electrical panel upgrade take?
faqs.a: A standard panel upgrade typically takes one to two days, though timing can be coordinated to align with your addition's overall construction schedule.

faqs.q: Can I add new circuits without upgrading my panel?
faqs.a: Only if your existing panel has enough spare capacity. An assessment will confirm whether new circuits can be added safely or require an upgrade first.

faqs.q: When should I schedule an electrical assessment for my addition?
faqs.a: During the design phase, before construction begins, so any panel upgrade can be planned and budgeted into the project from the start.
